Q58210: Famous for Jinhua ham, a dry-cured ham made for over 1,000 years.
Includes Yiwu, the world's biggest small-goods market, and Hengdian, China's 'Hollywood' film studio town.
Q34600: Former imperial capital of Japan (794–1868), in the Kansai region.
Has about 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines; 17 sites are part of a World Heritage listing.
Famous sights include Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion), Fushimi Inari's red torii gates and the Gion geisha district.
Spared from bombing in WWII; the 1997 Kyoto Protocol on climate change was signed here.
Q570829: City in southeastern Inner Mongolia; the name means 'red mountain'.
Gave its name to the Neolithic Hongshan culture, known for jade 'pig-dragons'.
Part of the old Liao dynasty heartland.
Q183124: Bolivia's fourth city, in a fertile Andean valley at about 2,500 m.
Called the 'City of Eternal Spring' for its mild climate.
Known for the Cristo de la Concordia statue, taller than Rio's Christ the Redeemer.
The 2000 'Water War' here reversed the privatisation of the city's water supply.
Q79754: Santiago de Querétaro is the capital of the state of Querétaro, in Mexico's Bajío region.
Its colonial centre and long stone aqueduct are a World Heritage Site.
The 1917 Mexican Constitution was written here; Emperor Maximilian was executed here in 1867.
Today a booming aerospace and manufacturing hub.
Q373101: Port city on the Yellow Sea in Shandong; the name means 'sunshine'.
Known for green policies: most homes use solar water heaters.
Has a big port for iron ore and coal and long sandy beaches.
Q72: Switzerland's largest city, at the northern end of Lake Zurich.
A global financial centre with major banks and the Swiss stock exchange.
Home of ETH Zurich, where Einstein studied; the Dada art movement began here in 1916.
Often ranked one of the most liveable — and most expensive — cities in the world.
Q167436: Capital of Paraíba in northeast Brazil.
Has the easternmost point of the Americas, Ponta do Seixas.
Founded in 1585, one of the oldest cities in Brazil; renamed after a murdered governor in 1930.
Known for its green spaces and beaches; a UNESCO City of Crafts.
Q110218: Tanzania's second-largest city, on the southern shore of Lake Victoria.
Nicknamed 'Rock City' for the granite boulders all around it; Bismarck Rock stands in the lake.
A centre of the Lake Victoria fishing industry (Nile perch) and gold mining in the region.
Q55741: City in Pampanga, central Luzon, at the core of Metro Clark.
Next to the former US Clark Air Base, now Clark Freeport Zone with an international airport.
Damaged by the 1991 eruption of nearby Mount Pinatubo.
Known as a culinary centre: sisig was invented here.
Q9365: Capital of Tajikistan, in the Hisar Valley.
Grew from a village with a Monday market — 'Dushanbe' means Monday in Tajik.
Has one of the world's tallest flagpoles and a huge teahouse and national library.
Q372414: City on the Yellow River delta on the Bohai Sea coast of Shandong.
Built around the Shengli Oil Field, China's second-largest.
The Yellow River Delta wetland reserve is a major bird habitat.
Q71227: Home of Dongfeng Motor, which built its first truck factory here in 1969 — 'China's Car City'.
The Wudang Mountains, a Taoist sacred site and birthplace of Wudang kung fu, are in the prefecture.
Danjiangkou reservoir supplies water to Beijing through the South–North Water Transfer.
Q202162: Commercial city in Abia State in southeastern Nigeria.
Famous for its craftsmen and the huge Ariaria International Market; 'Made in Aba' shoes and clothes.
The 1929 Aba Women's War was a major protest against British colonial taxation.
Q485918: Its name combines the counties Liuzhi, Panzhou and Shuicheng.
Called the 'Cool City' for its mild summers at high altitude.
Q416544: City in northwest Hunan on the Yuan River near Dongting Lake.
Said to be the site of 'Peach Blossom Spring', Tao Yuanming's famous story of a hidden paradise (Taoyuan county).
Has a long riverside wall of poetry carvings.
Was a battlefield of the 1943 Battle of Changde.
Q140304: Capital of Sharqia Governorate in the eastern Nile Delta.
Next to Bubastis (Tell Basta), the ancient city of the cat goddess Bastet.
A centre of the cotton and grain trade; home of Zagazig University.
Q42308: Ukraine's second city, in the northeast near the Russian border.
Capital of Soviet Ukraine from 1919 to 1934.
Its constructivist Derzhprom building was one of the first Soviet skyscrapers.
A major university, science and industrial centre; heavily shelled since 2022.
Q3711: Capital of Serbia, where the Sava flows into the Danube; the name means 'White City'.
One of the oldest cities in Europe, near the Vinča culture sites.
Its Kalemegdan fortress has been fought over many times; the city was destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times.
Capital of Yugoslavia during the 20th century.
Q243766: Capital of Santander department in Colombia.
Called the 'City of Parks' for its more than 160 parks.
Famous for eating hormigas culonas (big-bottomed ants).
Q29962: The largest city of Upper Egypt, on the Nile.
Has one of the largest Coptic Christian communities in Egypt.
Ancient Lycopolis, a centre of the jackal god Wepwawet; the philosopher Plotinus came from here.
The Asyut Barrage across the Nile dates from 1903.
Q200663: The most populous city in Haryana, a satellite city south of Delhi.
Founded in 1607 by Sheikh Farid, treasurer of Mughal emperor Jahangir.
A big industrial centre (tractors, motorcycles, auto parts).
Includes the Surajkund area, known for its yearly crafts fair.
Q1748: Capital of Denmark, on the islands of Zealand and Amager.
Grew from a Viking fishing village; capital since the early 15th century.
Famous for Nyhavn's coloured houses, the Little Mermaid statue and Tivoli Gardens (1843).
A world leader in cycling; connected to Malmö, Sweden, by the Øresund Bridge.
Q571766: Port city in Guangxi on the Gulf of Tonkin.
Home of the Beibu Gulf port and big petrochemical industry.
Known for Nixing pottery, one of China's four famous potteries, and for white dolphins nearby.
Q49261: The third-largest city in Arizona, part of the Phoenix metro area.
The largest US city that is not a county seat.
Founded by Mormon settlers in 1878; home of one of the first Mormon temples outside Utah.
Spring training ground for the Chicago Cubs baseball team.
Q1085: Capital of the Czech Republic on the Vltava River; the 'City of a Hundred Spires'.
Capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia and seat of Holy Roman Emperors like Charles IV and Rudolf II.
Prague Castle is one of the largest castle complexes in the world; the Charles Bridge and the astronomical clock are famous.
Scene of the 1968 Prague Spring and the 1989 Velvet Revolution.
Q1207076: County-level city in Shandong under Zaozhuang.
Site of the ancient State of Teng.
Probably the birthplace of the philosopher Mozi, who taught universal love; a memorial hall honours him.
Q13139252: Provincial capital at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River, just south of Bangkok.
Home of the Ancient City (Mueang Boran), one of the largest open-air museums in the world.
Suvarnabhumi Airport, Bangkok's main airport, is in the province.
Has a famous crocodile farm and the Erawan Museum with a three-headed elephant.
Q956602: City in Chhattisgarh, forming one urban area with Bhilai.
Bhilai is home to the Bhilai Steel Plant, built with Soviet help in the 1950s, India's main producer of rails.
Second-largest urban area of the state after Raipur.
Q3876: Capital of Malawi, in the central region on the Lilongwe River.
Replaced Zomba as capital in 1975, planned as a garden city.
Divided into an Old Town and a newer City Centre (Capital Hill).
Q5112: Capital of South Australia, between the Gulf St Vincent and the Mount Lofty Ranges.
Founded in 1836 as a planned city for free settlers (not convicts); surrounded by parklands.
Named after Queen Adelaide; known as the 'City of Churches'.
Gateway to the Barossa Valley wine region and holds the Adelaide Fringe festival.
Q170573: Holy city of Shia Islam, about 140 km south of Tehran.
Pilgrims visit the shrine of Fatima Masumeh, sister of the eighth Imam.
The world's largest centre of Shia religious scholarship; Ayatollah Khomeini taught here.
Known for a pistachio-brittle sweet called sohan.
Q8818: Spain's third city, on the Mediterranean, capital of the Valencian Community.
Founded by the Romans in 138 BC; its cathedral claims to hold the Holy Grail.
Home of paella and the Las Fallas festival, where giant figures are burned in March.
The City of Arts and Sciences by Santiago Calatrava lies in the old riverbed of the Turia.
Q48338: City in Central Anatolia at the foot of the volcano Mount Erciyes.
Called Caesarea in antiquity, the capital of Cappadocia.
Known for pastırma (cured beef) and mantı dumplings, and as a business city ('Kayseri merchants').
Gateway to the Cappadocia rock landscape.
Q20714: Capital of Gyeonggi Province, about 30 km south of Seoul.
Its Hwaseong Fortress (1796), built by King Jeongjo, is a World Heritage Site.
Known as the 'City of Filial Piety' and for its grilled ribs (galbi).
Q168888: Capital of Alagoas in northeast Brazil, on the Atlantic.
Known for turquoise beaches and natural reef pools.
Has suffered land subsidence caused by rock-salt mining under several neighbourhoods.
Q75150: Port city in Liaoning on Liaodong Bay.
Opened as a treaty port (Newchwang) in 1861, the first in Northeast China.
Known for its hot springs at Xiongyue and magnesite mining.
Q360643: City in northern Anhui (not to be confused with Suzhou in Jiangsu).
The Grand Canal of the Sui and Tang dynasties ran through it.
Site of the Battle of Gaixia (202 BC), where Xiang Yu was defeated by Liu Bang.
Q126148: City in northern Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic.
An international zone run by foreign powers from 1923 to 1956, a haven for spies and writers like Paul Bowles and William Burroughs.
Birthplace of the medieval traveller Ibn Battuta.
Tanger Med is Africa's biggest port; a high-speed train links it to Casablanca.
Q2473939: Fast-growing suburb north of Cotonou in Benin.
Home of the University of Abomey-Calavi, Benin's main university.
Next to the lake village of Ganvié on Lake Nokoué.
Q156819: The largest city in Santa Catarina state in southern Brazil.
Founded in 1851 by German, Swiss and Norwegian immigrants; named after the Prince of Joinville.
Hosts the only Bolshoi Ballet school outside Russia and a big dance festival.
Called the 'City of Flowers' and the 'City of Bicycles'.
Q4668212: Town and local government area in Imo State, Nigeria.
Known for its Itu Aka cultural festival in Nguru every February.
Part of the densely populated Mbaise area of Igboland.
Q222279: Capital of South Kivu in eastern DR Congo, on the south shore of Lake Kivu.
Lies right across the Ruzizi River from Rwanda.
Gateway to Kahuzi-Biéga National Park with eastern lowland gorillas.
Repeatedly affected by conflict; taken by M23 rebels in 2025.
Q160450: Port city on Turkey's Black Sea coast.
Atatürk landed here on 19 May 1919 to begin the Turkish War of Independence.
Known for Bafra pide and its tobacco farms.
Q165972: Coastal city in Florida, about 50 km north of Miami.
Called the 'Venice of America' for its 300 km of canals.
Named after a 19th-century fort of the Seminole Wars.
Its Port Everglades is a major cruise port; famous as a spring break spot.
Q7786: Capital of Riau province on the Siak River in Sumatra; the name means 'new market'.
Centre of Indonesia's oil (the Minas field) and palm oil industries.
Riau Malay culture: the Siak Sultanate palace is nearby.
Q2750772: Commercial and industrial city in Anambra State, Nigeria.
Called the 'Japan of Africa' for its many local manufacturers.
Home of Innoson, Nigeria's first indigenous car maker.
Known for its huge motor-spare-parts market.
Q80985: City in northern Morocco, the country's spiritual and cultural capital.
Founded in the 8th century; the University of al-Qarawiyyin (859) is often called the oldest existing university in the world.
Its medina, Fes el-Bali, is one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world (World Heritage Site).
Famous for its leather tanneries; the fez hat is named after it.
Q16568: The most populous city in Florida, on the St. Johns River near the Atlantic.
The largest city by area in the contiguous United States after merging with Duval County in 1968.
A big US Navy and logistics hub.
Q1757: Capital of Finland, on the Gulf of Finland; called Helsingfors in Swedish.
Founded in 1550 by King Gustav I of Sweden; became capital under Russian rule in 1812.
Known for its neoclassical Senate Square, the sea fortress Suomenlinna (World Heritage Site) and saunas.
Hosted the 1952 Summer Olympics; officially bilingual (Finnish and Swedish).
Q1520: Capital of Kazakhstan since 1997, on the Ishim River in the steppe; the name means 'capital'.
Called Akmolinsk, Tselinograd and, from 2019 to 2022, Nur-Sultan.
Rebuilt with futuristic buildings like the Bayterek Tower and the tent-shaped Khan Shatyr.
One of the coldest capitals in the world, with winters below −30 °C.
Q23197: Capital of Tennessee, on the Cumberland River.
'Music City', the home of country music, with the Grand Ole Opry and Music Row.
Has a full-size replica of the Parthenon, earning it the name 'Athens of the South'.
Q3854: Burundi's largest city and economic capital, on the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika.
Was the capital until 2019, when the government decided to move it to Gitega.
Ships most of Burundi's coffee and tea; began as a German military post called Usumbura.
Q207754: City in central Tamil Nadu on the Kaveri River; also called Trichy.
The Rockfort, a temple on an 83 m high rock, dominates the city.
Srirangam island has the Ranganathaswamy Temple, one of the largest functioning Hindu temples in the world.
Capital of the early Cholas (at Uraiyur).
Q10086: City in southern Karnataka at the foot of the Chamundi Hills.
Capital of the Kingdom of Mysore under the Wadiyar dynasty for centuries.
The Mysore Palace is lit with about 100,000 bulbs during the Dasara festival.
Known for silk, sandalwood, yoga (Ashtanga) and Mysore pak sweets.
Q713357: County-level city under Wenzhou in Zhejiang.
A centre of private manufacturing, especially car parts.
Birthplace of Sun Yirang, a pioneer in reading the ancient oracle-bone script.
Q9361: Capital of Kyrgyzstan, at the foot of the Tian Shan mountains near Kazakhstan.
Grew from a Kokand fortress (Pishpek); called Frunze in Soviet times (1926–1991).
Has wide tree-lined Soviet boulevards and the Ala-Too Square.
Known for its bazaars, like Osh Bazaar.
Q9863: City in Tamil Nadu surrounded by the Eastern Ghats.
Has India's largest magnesite deposits and the Salem Steel Plant.
Famous for mangoes and sago (tapioca) production.
Gateway to the Yercaud hill station.
Q151958: City in Hunan on the east shore of Dongting Lake where it joins the Yangtze.
The Yueyang Tower is one of the 'Three Great Towers' of southern China, made famous by Fan Zhongyan's essay.
Junshan island in the lake grows the rare Junshan Yinzhen yellow tea.
Hunan's only Yangtze port open to international trade.
Q36433: Portugal's second city, on the Douro River near the Atlantic.
Gave its name to Portugal ('Portus Cale') and to port wine, aged in cellars across the river in Vila Nova de Gaia.
Its historic Ribeira district is a World Heritage Site; the Dom Luís I iron bridge is a landmark.
Home of FC Porto; Henry the Navigator was born here.
